fields.title: Cascade and Priorities
fields.keyTakeaway: A cascade is profitable with a low escalation rate and reliable result verification, when in doubt escalate up, and the model's self-assessment should not be trusted.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Can we use a cheap model for most requests, and an expensive one only when needed?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A cascade provides multiple-fold savings, but introduces a new class of errors: misjudging complexity sends a difficult request to a weak model. It is designed by the product team because the decision of "what to do when uncertain" is a product one.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: **[[model-cascade|Model cascade]]** — cheap model first, expensive model upon uncertainty.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: Three ways to determine that an expensive one is needed:
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: *Pre-call classification.* A separate small model or rules estimate complexity. Cheap, makes mistakes. *Self-assessment.* The cheap model answers and estimates confidence. Models are poorly calibrated, use with caution. *Result verification.* Programmatic check of the cheap model's response: is the format maintained, are mandatory parts present, did it pass validation. Most reliable where the result is structural.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Product rule: **when in doubt, escalate up.** The cost of an unnecessary expensive call is lower than the cost of a bad response.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: The economic effect depends on the escalation rate. At 20% escalations and a 10x price difference, the cascade saves about 70%. At 60% escalations, it makes almost no sense.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: A separate scheme is **splitting by user rather than by request.** Paying users get the strong model, everyone else gets the weak one. Simple, predictable, but means different product quality for different people, and that is a product decision with consequences for perception.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: The cascade was applied in one feature — extracting ingredients from supplier descriptions.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The small model extracts the structure. Programmatic check: did the JSON parse, are mandatory fields filled, are values plausible? On failure — the medium model. On repeated failure — manual handling.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Escalation rate 17%, manual processing 1.2%. Catalog processing cost dropped about 4 times.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: It works well here because the result is structural and checked programmatically. For generating user responses, we did not use a cascade: there is no reliable way to evaluate response quality before showing it, and we do not trust the model's self-assessment.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Splitting by users was discussed and rejected: the assistant is part of the core product, different quality for paying and non-paying users contradicts positioning. We would return to the question if a paid subscription appears.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: A cascade complicates debugging and evals: the result depends on which path the request took. Metrics must be calculated separately per path.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A cascade is profitable with a low escalation rate and reliable result verification, when in doubt escalate up, and the model's self-assessment should not be trusted.
